title: "report." and "report " are the same file as "report" on Windows, but not to your path library
assumption: Two filename strings that differ only by a trailing dot or space refer to two different files.

input.description: A filename built by concatenating a title with a trailing space, or a name ending in a stray period from a stripped extension.

what_goes_wrong: A dedup or uniqueness check built on string comparison treats "report." and "report" as different names, but Win32 silently drops the trailing dot/space when it actually creates the file, so the second create overwrites the first, or the app can't find the file it thinks it just wrote.
why: Win32 normalizes almost every path it is given (the same step GetFullPathName performs), and one rule of that normalization is that when the path does not end in a separator, trailing periods and spaces are removed from the last component. Only paths that start with the \\?\ prefix skip that step, which is why a file named "report." can exist on NTFS yet be unreachable by ordinary programs. Pure path libraries perform no such rewrite; PureWindowsPath and path.win32 preserve the trailing characters exactly and report the strings as different, the opposite of what Windows will do with them.
affects: windows win32 path normalization (strips trailing dots and spaces unless the path starts with \\?\)

repros.code:
from pathlib import PureWindowsPath
a = PureWindowsPath("C:/Users/me/report.")
b = PureWindowsPath("C:/Users/me/report")
c = PureWindowsPath("C:/Users/me/report ")
print(a.name, "==", b.name, "?", a == b)
print(repr(c.name), "==", repr(b.name), "?", c == b)

repros.note: Creating "report." or "report " through the normal Win32 CreateFile path creates or opens "report": normalization drops the trailing dot or space before the filesystem sees the name, so both strings collide with a plain "report".

fix: Strip trailing dots and spaces from each user-supplied name component yourself before comparing, storing or creating it, matching what Win32 normalization will do anyway; or reject such names outright.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: File path formats on Windows systems (Trim characters)
Microsoft Learn: Naming Files, Paths, and Namespaces

test_cases.note: A filename-key function meant to be safe on Windows should map these to the same key, because Windows will create the same file for both.
